summary: Describes the file format used by snoop, Sun's packet monitoring and capture program, so people can write compatible programs. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A description of how a packet-watching tool saves what it saw so others can read the file.

what is the snoop file identification pattern
subtitle: How Sun's snoop tool stores captured network packets on disk, so other programs can read and write the same files.

tldr.problem: Capturing packets and analysing them later is very useful for debugging networks, but other programs could not read or create snoop's capture files without knowing their layout.
tldr.mechanism: A snoop file is a fixed File Header followed by one or more Packet Records. Each record has 24 octets of descriptive information, the captured packet data and optional padding.
tldr.outcome: Anyone can write programs that generate or interpret snoop version 2 capture files. The memo is Informational and defines no Internet standard.

today: RFC 1761 is an Informational memo with no obsoleting or updating RFC listed. It documents a vendor's file format and does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: Why Capture Files Matter
sections.content:
Tools that capture, display and interpret packets are very useful for debugging network problems. Saving captured packets to a file separates two jobs: collecting information about a problem, and analysing it later.

snoop is a packet monitoring and capture program developed by Sun. This memo describes the file format it uses so that others can write programs that interpret snoop capture files, or create files that snoop can interpret.
sections.plainLanguage: If you record a show, you can watch it later instead of live. Snoop records network traffic so people can study it afterwards.

sections.title: File Layout and File Header
sections.content:
A snoop capture file is an array of octets. It starts with a fixed-length File Header, followed by one or more variable-length Packet Records, each holding the data of one captured packet.

The File Header has three parts. The Identification Pattern is 8 octets, 73 6E 6F 6F 70 00 00 00, which is the ASCII string snoop followed by three null octets. The Version Number is a 32-bit unsigned integer; this document describes version 2, and version 1 was used in early implementations and is now obsolete. The Datalink Type is a 32-bit field that says what kind of datalink header the packet records use.
sections.plainLanguage: Every recording starts with a label that says 'this is a snoop tape', which version it is, and what kind of network it came from. After the label come the recorded packets, one after another.

sections.title: The Packet Record
sections.content:
Each packet record holds a partial or complete copy of one packet and some descriptive information. The packet may be truncated to limit how much is stored, and the record may be padded so it aligns on a convenient machine-dependent boundary.

The descriptive information is 24 octets, made of six 32-bit integers: Original Length (the packet's length as received from the network), Included Length (how much of it is stored; smaller than the original if the packet was truncated), Packet Record Length (the whole record, including the 24 octets, the data and the pad), Cumulative Drops, Timestamp Seconds and Timestamp Microseconds.

Cumulative Drops counts packets lost by the capturing system between the first record in the file and this one. Some implementations cannot count drops and may set it to zero. The timestamp is in seconds since January 1, 1970, plus microseconds. After the six integers comes the Packet Data, beginning with its datalink header, then a Pad of zero or more octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Each recorded packet comes with a little tag: how big it really was, how much was saved, how many were missed, and when it arrived. Then comes the packet itself, with a bit of empty space at the end if needed.

sections.title: Byte Order and Security
sections.content:
All integer values are stored in big-endian order, with the high-order bits first. A reader on any machine must account for this when reading the lengths, counters and timestamps.

The memo's Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: When writing a big number, everyone must agree which digit goes first. Snoop always writes the biggest part first. The memo says nothing about safety.

fields.name: Original Length
fields.desc: Length in octets of the packet as received from the network.

fields.name: Included Length
fields.desc: Length of the Packet Data field; less than Original Length if truncated.

fields.name: Packet Record Length
fields.desc: Total record length: 24 octets, packet data and pad.

fields.name: Cumulative Drops
fields.desc: Packets lost since the first record in the file.

fields.name: Timestamp Seconds
fields.desc: Seconds since January 1, 1970 when the packet arrived.
